title: A King Arrives on a Donkey
overview: Jesus enters Jerusalem to cheers as a king, disrupts the temple, and clashes with the religious leaders over who gave him the right to act this way.

parts.label: Entering Jerusalem (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: Riding a donkey acts out Zechariah's picture of a gentle king who comes in peace, not on a war horse, and cloaks and branches on the road were a royal welcome. "Hosanna" first meant "save us" and became a shout of praise, while "Son of David" named the king people hoped God would send.

parts.label: Clearing the temple (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Traders sold animals for sacrifice and changed coins into temple money, and Jesus uses words from Isaiah and Jeremiah to say a house of prayer had become a hideout for robbers. He then heals the blind and lame there, and when leaders object to children praising him, he answers with a line from Psalm 8.

parts.label: The withered fig tree (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: Many interpreters read this as an acted warning about the temple, which looked full of life but bore no real fruit. Jesus then turns the moment into a lesson about praying with trust.

parts.label: A question about authority (vv. 23-27)
parts.note: When the leaders ask who authorized him, he asks whether John the Baptist's mission came from God or from people. Either answer would cost them, by exposing their unbelief or angering crowds who saw John as a prophet, so they say they don't know.

parts.label: Two sons (vv. 28-32)
parts.note: One son refuses but then works, and the other agrees but never goes, so what counts is doing, not saying. Tax collectors, seen as cheats working for Rome, and prostitutes responded to John and changed, while the respected leaders did not.

parts.label: The vineyard tenants (vv. 33-46)
parts.note: Building on Isaiah's picture of Israel as God's vineyard, the tenants stand for the leaders and the mistreated servants for the prophets, and Christians read the murdered son as Jesus himself. A line from Psalm 118 says the stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone, the key stone of a building, and the leaders realized the story was aimed at them.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jesus' warning in verse 43 that the kingdom of God will be taken away is aimed only at the leaders he was speaking to, or means God's people were redefined around the church, a reading that has been used against Jewish people and that many now reject.
think: When one person says the right things but never follows through, and another refuses at first but then comes around, which one do you trust more, and why?
